bib.title: MetaCogAgent: A Metacognitive Multi-Agent LLM Framework with Self-Aware Task Delegation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MetaCogAgent: A Metacognitive Multi-Agent LLM Framework with Self-Aware Task Delegation", Chenyu Wang and Yang Shu. arXiv 2605.17292v1, 17 May 2026. It is a preprint with an IEEE SMC-style format. The text says the code and benchmark "will be released upon publication".

COVERAGE: All 31,069 of 31,069 chars were read, including the abstract, tables I-V, discussion, limitations and references. The PDF has no appendices. I did not run the figure-caption script, because Fig. 1-3 are visible in the extraction.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- **Headline accuracy.** MetaCogAgent reaches 82.4% on its own benchmark. That is 5.3 points above Majority-Vote (77.1%) and 8.7 points above AutoGen (73.7%). Single-Agent scores 65.3%.
  - number: 82.4%
  - setup: MetaCog-Eval, 700 tasks. N=3 prompted GPT-4 agents (reasoning, retrieval, coding). Single run.
  - quote: "MetaCogAgent achieves the highest task accuracy of 82.4%, surpassing the strongest baseline (Majority-V ote, 77.1%) by 5.3 percentage points and the best routing baseline (AutoGen, 73.7%) by 8.7 points."
  - where: Sec. V-B, Table II

- **Call counts.** MetaCogAgent uses 1382 API calls against 700 for Single-Agent, 1456 for AutoGen and 2100 for Majority-Vote. The "34% fewer than ensemble" figure is relative to a 3-agent vote that costs 3x.
  - number: 1382 vs 2100 calls
  - setup: calls are counted per task over the 700-task set. The authors call this "a coarse efficiency proxy" and note that token usage is not counted.
  - quote: "MetaCogAgent uses only 1382 API calls—5.1% fewer than AutoGen (1456) while achieving 8.7% higher accuracy, and 34% fewer than the brute-force Majority-V ote (2100)."
  - where: Sec. V-B, Table II

- **Ablation.** Removing adaptive delegation drops accuracy by 5.1 points, to 77.3%. That is about the same as Majority-Vote (77.1%). Removing self-assessment costs 6.8 points and removing boundary learning costs 3.2.
  - number: 77.3% (−5.1)
  - setup: same benchmark, single run
  - quote: "Removing Adaptive Delegation (agents always execute assigned tasks) reduces accuracy by 5.1%, showing the value of task re-routing."
  - where: Sec. V-E, Table IV (the 77.3 row)

- **Where it helps.** The gain over AutoGen is largest on Hard tasks (+13) and cross-domain tasks (+13). Delegation rates rise from 10.5% (Easy) to 41.5% (Hard), and 218 of 700 tasks (31.1%) were delegated.
  - number: 11.5-point Easy-to-Hard drop vs 18.5 for Single-Agent
  - quote: "MetaCogAgent's degradation is the smallest (11.5% drop vs. 18.5% for Single-Agent)."
  - setup: Table III, same agents
  - where: Sec. V-C, V-G

- **Calibration.** ECE is 0.087 for MetaCogAgent against 0.194 for Single-Agent. ECE is 0.051 on Easy tasks and 0.132 on Hard tasks.
  - number: 0.087
  - quote: "Calibration is strongest for Easy tasks (ECE=0.051) and degrades for Hard tasks (ECE=0.132)"
  - setup: 10-bin reliability diagram, Fig. 3
  - where: Sec. V-F

- **Condition for gains.** The authors expect gains only when agents differ in competence. This is an expectation, not something they tested.
  - number: none
  - quote: "We expect the largest gains under strong capability asymmetry and the smallest when agents are near-identical."
  - setup: Sec. VI. Note that all three agents are the same GPT-4 with different system prompts.
  - where: Sec. VI, "Generalizability"

IS IT COMPUTE-MATCHED? No.
- **No matched self-consistency baseline.** There is no single-model self-consistency baseline at about 1382 calls.
- **Cost mismatch with Single-Agent.** The comparison with Single-Agent (700 calls) is not cost-equal; MetaCogAgent uses about 2x the calls.
- **Majority-Vote is not a budget match.** The only voting baseline is 3 agents on every task (2100 calls). Its accuracy is lower, but its budget is higher, so this is not a matched comparison.
- **No best-single-model baseline.** The text does not name a best-single-model baseline; all agents are GPT-4.
- **Unclear call accounting.** The text does not break down how the 1382 calls are counted. It does not say whether the confidence queries to all agents and the Collaborative Mode votes are included.
- **Cheap baselines at a different budget.** Round-Robin, Random-Routing and Skill-Fixed all use 700 calls, so they sit at a different budget.

LIMITS
- **Concessions in the text:**
  - Only 3 agents were tested.
  - Profile learning assumes stationary competence.
  - GPT-4 generated the tasks and also executes them. Heterogeneous backbones and public benchmarks were not tested.
  - "All reported results are single-run" with no variance. The 1-3 point gaps in the ablation and sensitivity tables are therefore not separable from noise.
- **Further gaps (my reading):**
  - The benchmark is self-built, with optimal agent labels, so routing is scored against the authors' own labels.
  - Open-ended tasks are scored by a GPT-4 judge.
  - The Easy/Medium/Hard counts in Table I (200 each) appear to be 5 dimensions × about 40 tasks, which the text describes as "40 tasks each".
  - The dispatcher is round-robin, so the "best routing baseline" is AutoGen, which is not a router.
  - The code is not released, so the results are not reproducible.
- **Dated:** GPT-4 era baselines. No reasoning models.

CODE
- Confidence mix (Eq. 2): `ci(tk) = λ·cv + (1−λ)·cp`.
- Conflict-tightened threshold: `θ′ = θ + γ·δ`, applied when `δ = |cv − cp| > 0.3`.
- Profile update (Eq. 4): `p ← p + α(r − p)`, with α=0.1.
- Defaults: θ=0.5, λ=0.6, α=0.1, γ=0.2.

FIGURES: Fig. 1 (p. 2) is the architecture, showing the dispatcher, per-agent confidence scores, and the Delegation Hub that re-routes when c<θ′. It is the one candidate, because it shows the confidence-gated routing that adds calls only for delegated tasks. I did not render it.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. The extraction is clean apart from some garbled math symbols. The "8.7%" in the abstract means percentage points. The conclusion calls AutoGen the "best routing baseline", while Majority-Vote is the stronger baseline.
